footer: The Needham Question · East, West and the habit of asking · C1
title: The Needham Question
subtitle: A Cambridge biochemist learns Chinese from a colleague in 1938, spends the rest of his life asking one question — and, fifty years later, psychologists with a fish tank and a rice field think they have part of the answer.
crosslink: Read the story of the experiment that started this conversation: The Left-Handed Universe →
intention: you'll follow a true story about whether 'East' and 'West' really think differently about questions, evidence and contradiction — and learn to generalise the way good scientists do: tend to, on average, are more likely to, by no means all, it would be an oversimplification to say.
warmup: Describe a photograph you know well — a family picture, a famous image. What do you mention first: the person in the middle, or where they are and what surrounds them?
Two statements: 'Too much modesty is a fault' and 'Modesty is a virtue'. Can both be true? Do you feel pressure to choose?
China had printing, paper, gunpowder and the magnetic compass centuries before Europe. Why, then, did Galileo and Newton happen in Europe? Give a first guess — you'll test it later.
vocab_intro: Before we read, let's unlock the words you'll need — the vocabulary of thinking about thinking. Think first; the Reveal only confirms.

vocab.heading: A. Work it out from the sentence
vocab.instruction: Read each sentence aloud and say what the bold word means from the rest of the sentence. Then reveal.

items.sent: A holistic doctor does not treat the knee; she asks about your sleep, your job, your diet and your worries, because the knee is part of all of them.
items.meaning: holistic (adj) — treating something as a connected whole rather than a set of separate parts. (n: holism)

items.sent: An analytical mind takes a problem apart: isolate the one variable that matters, hold everything else still, and test it.
items.meaning: analytical (adj) — separating things into their parts in order to examine them. (n: analysis; v: analyse)

items.sent: In a rice village nobody can flood or drain the fields alone; every family is interdependent with its neighbours, whether it likes them or not.
To say 'Asians are holistic and Westerners are analytical' is an oversimplification: it takes a small average difference and turns it into two kinds of person.
items.meaning: an oversimplification (n) — a description that leaves out so much complexity that it becomes misleading. (v: to oversimplify)

vocab.heading: B. From the meaning to the word
vocab.instruction: Which word fits the definition? The first letter is given. Say the word, then reveal.

items.sent: A way of thinking that accepts that two opposing statements may both be partly true, and looks for the middle way between them. It begins with d.
items.meaning: dialectical (adj) — reasoning that holds opposites together and seeks a resolution between them. (n: dialectic)

items.sent: The system of officials, offices, rules and paperwork through which a state is run. It begins with b.
items.meaning: bureaucracy (n) — government by officials and administrative rules. (adj: bureaucratic)

items.sent: A general direction or inclination — not a rule, but what happens more often than not. It begins with t.
items.meaning: a tendency (n) — an inclination towards a particular kind of behaviour or result. a tendency to… (v: to tend to)

vocab.heading: C. Choose the meaning
vocab.instruction: One sentence, three options. Say a, b or c — then reveal.

items.sent: Asked what they had seen, the Americans described the focal fish first. Focal means: (a) fastest (b) central, the one attention is directed to (c) largest
items.meaning: (b) — focal (adj) — at the centre of attention or interest. (n: focus)

items.sent: Chinese students were more likely to endorse both of two contradictory arguments. To endorse is: (a) to reject (b) to misunderstand (c) to declare your support for or agreement with
items.meaning: (c) — to endorse (v) — to support or agree with publicly. (n: endorsement)

items.sent: That laws of nature exist and can be written down seemed self-evident to Newton; it was not self-evident everywhere. Self-evident means: (a) obvious without needing proof (b) secret (c) scientifically proven
items.meaning: (a) — self-evident (adj) — so obvious that it needs no proof or explanation.

vocab_use: Sort the ten words into ways of thinking, ways of organising a society, and ways of talking carefully.
Using holistic, analytical and oversimplification, predict what this story will claim — and what it will warn against.
story_intro: A true story in three parts — a man, a question, and the scientists who inherited it. Every experiment, date and number here is real. Read each part; after it, try the quick check from memory, then talk about the question.

story.title: Part 1 — Two characters for 'cigarette'
paras: In 1937 Joseph Needham was thirty-six, a Cambridge biochemist with a growing reputation, a wife who was also a distinguished scientist, and no particular interest in China. That autumn three young Chinese scientists arrived in his laboratory to do research. One of them was Lu Gwei-djen, the daughter of a pharmacist from Nanjing, who had trained in biochemistry and who had grown up with a knowledge Needham did not possess: that her civilisation had a scientific and technical past two thousand years deep.

In February 1938 he asked her how to say 'cigarette' in Chinese. She said xiangyan — fragrant smoke — and wrote the two characters, guiding his hand through the strokes. He later said it was the moment his life changed direction. Through 1938 and 1939 he studied Chinese with a passion that alarmed his colleagues, learned the classical language privately with the university's professor of Chinese, and began to read what Lu had told him about: treatises on astronomy, medicine and engineering that were older than anything comparable in Europe.

What he found unsettled everything he had been taught. Paper, printing, the magnetic compass, gunpowder — the four inventions that had, in Francis Bacon's phrase, changed the whole face of the world — were all Chinese, and so were cast iron, the stirrup, the wheelbarrow, the seismograph, and the recognition of sunspots and supernovae centuries before European astronomers accepted that the heavens could change. For most of recorded history China had been the more advanced civilisation. And yet the thing we call modern science — Galileo's experiments, Newton's laws, the idea that nature runs on mathematical rules that any person can test — had happened in a small corner of western Europe in the seventeenth century, and not in China.

Why? That was the question. Needham would spend the remaining fifty-seven years of his life trying to answer it, and it now carries his name: the Needham Question. What he did not yet know, in 1938, was that the question had a second half, and that the second half was about him. Why had a scientist as curious as Needham never once wondered about Chinese science until a colleague wrote two characters on a piece of paper?

check.q: What did Lu Gwei-djen give Needham, and what did his reading reveal?
check.a: First the Chinese characters for 'cigarette', then a language and a literature. His reading showed that for most of history China had been the more advanced civilisation — paper, printing, the compass, gunpowder, cast iron, the seismograph, records of sunspots — and yet modern science arose in seventeenth-century Europe.

check.q: State the Needham Question in one sentence — and its 'second half'.
check.a: Why did modern science develop in Europe and not in China, given China's earlier lead? And its second half: why had a curious Western scientist never thought to ask about Chinese science at all?

story.discuss: Needham was a brilliant, curious man, and China's scientific past was simply invisible to him until 1938. What makes a whole area of knowledge invisible to intelligent people? Is anything invisible to you in the same way?

story.title: Part 2 — Thirty thousand miles
paras: War gave him his chance. From 1942 to 1946 Needham ran the Sino-British Science Co-operation Office in Chongqing, the wartime capital, with the job of getting instruments, chemicals and journals to Chinese scientists cut off by the Japanese occupation. He turned it into an expedition. In lorries, on trains and on foot he travelled the length of unoccupied China — he put the distance at thirty thousand miles — visiting universities that had retreated inland and were teaching in temples and caves, and buying, begging and copying every old scientific text he could find. By the time he came home he had a library, a network of collaborators, and the outline of an answer.

The first volume of Science and Civilisation in China appeared in 1954. Needham planned seven volumes; the project has now passed twenty-seven, and it continued after his death. What he argued, across all of them, was that the Question could not be answered by saying that Chinese people thought differently. Chinese astronomers had observed more carefully than Europeans; Chinese engineers had built better; Chinese doctors had recorded more. The difference was not in the minds. It was in the arrangements around the minds.

His candidates were institutional. Imperial China was run by a scholar-bureaucracy selected by examination in the Confucian classics, which drew the ablest minds of every generation into administration and literature rather than into nature. Merchants — the class that in Europe paid for instruments, voyages and printing — were held in low esteem and kept under the state's thumb. And the Chinese picture of the cosmos was of an organism in harmony, not of a machine obeying laws; there was no divine lawgiver, and so, Needham suggested, the very idea that nature has 'laws' that a human being could discover and write down did not seem self-evident, as it did to Kepler and Newton. Europe, fragmented into competing states, quarrelling churches and free cities, could not stop new questions being asked; China, unified and stable, did not need to.

Needham died in 1995, aged ninety-four. His wife Dorothy had died in 1987, and in 1989, when he was eighty-eight, he married Lu Gwei-djen, who had worked beside him on the books for fifty years. The Question outlived them both. And in the decade after his death it was taken up, without anyone quite intending it, by a different kind of scientist entirely — psychologists, with laboratories, questionnaires and a fish tank.

check.q: What did Needham do in China during the war, and what came of it?
check.a: He ran the Sino-British Science Co-operation Office in Chongqing (1942–46), travelled some thirty thousand miles across unoccupied China supplying scientists and collecting old texts, and returned with the material for Science and Civilisation in China — first volume 1954, now more than twenty-seven volumes.

check.q: Summarise Needham's answer: where did the difference lie, according to him?
check.a: Not in minds but in institutions: an examination-selected scholar-bureaucracy that absorbed talent; merchants kept weak; a cosmos seen as a harmonious organism rather than a law-governed machine, so 'laws of nature' were not self-evident; and a unified, stable state with no competition of the kind that forced Europe to tolerate new questions.

story.discuss: Needham refused the easy answer — 'they thought differently' — and looked at exams, merchants and government instead. Which kind of explanation do you instinctively reach for when you see two groups behave differently: their minds, or their circumstances?

story.title: Part 3 — The fish tank and the rice field
paras: In 2001 Takahiko Masuda and Richard Nisbett showed twenty-second animated underwater scenes to students at Kyoto University and the University of Michigan: a large, fast, brightly coloured fish in the foreground; smaller fish, plants, bubbles, rocks behind. Then they asked what the students had seen. The Americans tended to begin with the big fish — the star of the scene. The Japanese tended to begin with the setting: the water was green, the bottom was rocky, there were plants. On average they mentioned around sixty-five per cent more background detail than the Americans did. Shown the big fish again against a new background, the Americans recognised it easily; the Japanese, more often, did not — for them the fish had been part of a whole, and the whole had changed.

Nisbett and his colleagues found the same shape again and again. Kaiping Peng gave Chinese and American students pairs of arguments that contradicted each other; the Americans tended to pick one and strengthen it, the Chinese more often accepted that both had something in them and looked for a middle way — a habit Peng called dialectical thinking, and which he found in the proverbs each group preferred. Heejung Kim asked Asian-American and European-American students to solve reasoning problems while thinking aloud; talking made no difference to the European Americans and made the Asian Americans worse, because, she argued, one tradition assumes that speech is thinking and the other assumes that thinking is done in silence. Nisbett gathered all of it in a book called The Geography of Thought, and for a while it looked as though the Needham Question had a psychological answer after all: the West isolates the object and asks what rule it obeys; the East sees the field and asks how everything fits. Analytical minds invent physics. Holistic minds invent harmony.

Then the story became more interesting. In 2014 Thomas Talhelm and colleagues tested 1,162 Han Chinese students from across China on the same measures — and found the 'East–West' difference inside China. Students from the wheat-growing north thought in the more analytical, individualist way; students from the rice-growing south thought more holistically and interdependently. Rice needs irrigation and cooperation; wheat can be grown by a family alone. The differences between neighbouring counties on either side of the rice–wheat line were as large as the differences psychologists had reported between Japan and America. It was not 'Eastern culture' that produced holistic thinking. It was, at least in part, what your ancestors had to do together to eat.

And the tidy story had another problem, which any physics student can see. Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang, who in 1956 asked whether an assumption every Western physicist had accepted for thirty years had ever been tested, were born in Shanghai and Hefei. Chien-Shiung Wu, who broke it, was born near Shanghai. The most analytical, rule-breaking question of the mid-twentieth century was asked by three people whose culture, according to the book, sees fields rather than fish. Perhaps the differences are real, and average, and small, and shaped by rice and exams and lawgivers and a hundred other things; and perhaps the habit that makes a scientist — noticing that a fact is really an assumption, and asking whether anyone has checked — belongs to no hemisphere at all. Needham, who learned it from two characters on a piece of paper, would probably have agreed.

check.q: Describe the fish-tank result and one of the other two experiments.
check.a: Michigan students tended to describe the focal fish first and recognised it against new backgrounds; Kyoto students described the setting first, mentioned about sixty-five per cent more background detail, and were less likely to recognise the fish out of context. Peng: Chinese students more often endorsed both sides of a contradiction; Kim: thinking aloud hurt Asian-American but not European-American reasoning.

check.q: What did Talhelm's rice–wheat study add, and why does the story end with Lee, Yang and Wu?
check.a: It found the same analytical/holistic difference inside China, between wheat-growing north and rice-growing south, as large across a county line as between Japan and America — so 'Eastern culture' is not the cause. Lee, Yang and Wu, Chinese-born, asked and answered the most analytical question of their era, so the habit of questioning belongs to no hemisphere.

story.discuss: The psychologists' differences are real, measured, and — on average — small. What is the right way to hold a true generalisation about millions of people in your head without turning it into a verdict on the person in front of you?

grammar.h2: The grammar this story runs on: generalising without stereotyping
grammar.intro: Every claim in Part 3 is about averages: the Japanese tended to…, Americans were more likely to…. Say the same thing without the hedge — Japanese people see backgrounds — and a finding becomes a stereotype. At C1 you are expected to make general claims. The grammar of hedging is what lets you make them honestly.
notes:
1. Verbs and phrases of tendency.
• tend to + verb: "Northern students tended to think more analytically."
• be more / less likely to: "Americans were more likely to recognise the fish."
• have a tendency to / show a tendency towards: "…a tendency towards dialectical answers."

2. Adverbials that mark the scope of a claim.
• on average · in general · as a rule · by and large · to some extent · in part
• Quantifiers instead of 'all': most, many, a majority of, a significant proportion of.
• "On average, Japanese participants mentioned more background detail" — true. "Japanese people notice backgrounds" — not what the study showed.

3. Limiting and correcting the generalisation.
• by no means all / not every / far from: "By no means all southern students were holistic thinkers."
• This does not mean (that)… / It does not follow that…: "It does not follow that an individual from Kyoto will…"
• It would be an oversimplification / a mistake to say that… · The picture is more complicated: · with the important exception of…

exercises.instruction: One each, from: tended to · on average · by no means all · it does not follow that · a significant proportion of.
items: The Kyoto students ___ begin their descriptions with the setting rather than the fish.
___, they mentioned around sixty-five per cent more background detail.
___ rice-region students were holistic thinkers; many were not.
Two groups differ on average, but ___ any individual will fit the pattern.
___ Chinese students endorsed both sides of the contradiction — but so did some Americans.

exercises.h3: Turn the stereotype back into a finding
exercises.instruction: Each sentence overstates what the research showed. Rewrite it honestly, using at least one hedge. Say it, then reveal a model.
items: Asians think holistically and Westerners think analytically.
Chinese people can't handle contradiction; Americans can't handle nuance.
Thinking aloud doesn't work for Asian students.
Southern Chinese are collectivists because they grow rice.
China didn't invent modern science because Chinese people don't ask questions.
answers: In the studies, East Asian participants tended, on average, to attend more to context, and Americans more to focal objects — a difference of degree, not of kind.
Chinese students were more likely to endorse both sides of a contradiction, and Americans more likely to choose one; it does not follow that either group 'can't' do the other.
In one experiment, thinking aloud impaired the performance of Asian-American students on average, while European-American students were unaffected; by no means all individuals responded that way.

Talhelm's study found that students from rice-growing regions showed a tendency towards more interdependent thinking; the researchers proposed that a history of cooperative farming explains part of the difference.
It would be an oversimplification to say Chinese people don't ask questions — Needham argued the causes were institutional, and Lee, Yang and Wu asked the most searching question of their era.

exercises.h3: Put it together — a fair summary in one paragraph
exercises.instruction: Fill each gap with the hedge the hint asks for. Read it aloud — it should sound like a careful scientist, not a travel guide.
items: Psychologists have found that East Asian participants ___ (tend to) attend to context, whereas Americans ___ (be more likely to) focus on a central object. ___ (on average), the differences are consistent, but they are small, and ___ (by no means all) participants fit the pattern. ___ (it does not follow that) a particular person will think one way because of where they were born; indeed, Talhelm found differences ___ (to some extent) as large within China as between China and America. ___ (it would be an oversimplification to say that) the West asks questions and the East seeks harmony.
answers: tend to · are more likely to · On average · by no means all · It does not follow that · to some extent · It would be an oversimplification to say that

grammar.outro: In the Speak tab you'll argue about East and West for four minutes — and every generalisation you make will need a hedge or a limit, or your partner will catch you stereotyping.

deeper.h2: Why this story stays with you
paras: The Needham Question has never been answered, and the best modern historians think it may be the wrong shape: it assumes that modern science was the natural destination of any advanced civilisation, and asks why China 'failed' to arrive, when the strange event that needs explaining is arguably that it happened anywhere at all. But Needham's instinct — to look at examinations, merchants and cosmologies rather than at 'the Chinese mind' — has aged far better than the psychology that briefly seemed to replace it. Talhelm's rice line runs through the middle of China; Nisbett's own later work stressed that the differences are habits, not abilities, and shift within a generation of migration or education.

There is a smaller lesson inside the large one, and it is about classrooms. Kim's experiment suggests that a student raised to believe that thinking happens in silence may perform worse when forced to talk their way through a problem — and that a teacher who takes silence for absence may be wrong. Any language lesson is an exercise in thinking aloud in a foreign tongue. Knowing that the habit of doing so is itself cultural, and learnable, changes how you feel about the pause before you answer.
deeper.note: Look again at the two characters. Needham's life turned on a colleague writing 'fragrant smoke' on a piece of paper. Lu Gwei-djen gave him a language; the language gave him a library; the library gave him a question. How much of what any of us knows depends on who happened to sit at the next bench?
questions: Needham says the difference was institutional; Nisbett says it is cognitive; Talhelm says it is agricultural. Are these rival answers, or layers of the same one? Which would you test first, and how?
'Analytical minds invent physics; holistic minds invent harmony.' Find the sentence in the story that destroys this — then ask whether it destroys it completely.
Peng's dialectical thinkers accept that two contradictory statements can both be true. Is that wisdom, or the refusal to decide? When is each?
Kim's finding — that being made to talk can make some students think worse — is about you, now, in this lesson. Do you think in words? In a second language? Does speaking help you or cost you?

speak.useful: Generalising honestly: "…tend to…", "…are more likely to…", "on average", "by no means all", "it does not follow that…", "it would be an oversimplification to say…". Weighing explanations: "One explanation is… but that leaves unexplained…", "The evidence points towards…".

tasks.label: Task A · Tell the whole story (4 minutes)
paras: Tell 'The Needham Question' to someone who has never heard of it: Cambridge 1937 and the two characters → what Needham found → the Question → thirty thousand miles and twenty-seven volumes → his institutional answer → the fish tank, the contradictions, thinking aloud → the rice line → Lee, Yang and Wu.
Every generalisation must carry a hedge, and use at least five key words (holistic, analytical, interdependent, oversimplification, dialectical, bureaucracy, tendency, focal, endorse, self-evident).

tasks.label: Task B · The debate (4 minutes)
paras: Motion: 'Modern science could only have begun in the West.' Argue for it using Needham's institutions and Nisbett's fish; then argue against it using Talhelm's rice line, Chinese inventions, and three physicists born in Shanghai and Hefei. Your listener stops you every time you generalise without a hedge.

tasks.label: Task C · Two ways of seeing (4 minutes)
paras: Describe one scene, situation or problem twice: first analytically — isolate the central thing and the rule it follows — then holistically — the whole field and how the parts depend on each other. Then say which description was more useful, and for what.
menu: A football goal: the striker's finish, or the movement of eleven players that created the space.
A photograph of a crowded street market.
A company's success: the founder, or the market, the timing and the team.
A school exam result: the student's effort, or the family, the teacher, the timetable and the weather that week.
A traffic jam, from the point of view of one driver and then from a helicopter.
A scientific discovery you know — the person who made it, or everything that had to be in place for it.

final: Needham never found out whether Chinese science 'failed' or European science was a freak event. Which framing do you find more convincing — and which is more flattering to whoever is asking?
If thinking styles are shaped by rice and wheat and exams, they can be changed. Should a school try to teach the other style? Which would you want more of?
Is 'East versus West' itself an analytical way of thinking — taking a whole world and cutting it into two objects?
Before you go — from memory: make three true claims about the research, each with a different hedge — one with tend to, one with on average, one with it does not follow that.
